summary: A nested-file child's identity is its host-qualified address, not a corpus-wide `kind:name` — so two hosts may each carry a `home`, and it resolves where the grammar says

edit.description: `NestedFileUnit` carries the host member's identity — the host kind and the host member's name — beside the host unit directory it already carries; both are in hand at `discover_nested_file`'s loop (the host kind it iterates, and the unit directory `unit_dir` cut the name from).

The nested-file arm of `resolve_kind_units` composes each child unit's id as the whole `<host-address>/<kind>/<key>` address the grammar gives a nested member, so identity is host-scoped rather than corpus-wide by name; the three `host_address(&kind.name, &unit.id)` sites (the manifest host, the satisfies match, the local-member list) go through the one address home instead of colon-joining a kind onto an id that is already an address.

One home for 'the member address this identity spells': the id verbatim when it already parses as a nested address, `host_address(kind, id)` otherwise. The discrimination exists today inside `graph::render_node`; lifting it here gives every caller the one rule (`specs/process/engineering.md`, 'One job, one home').

`lower_layout_reading`'s `let host = host_address(kind, name)` (2151) is the emit-side twin of the same decision — `compose.rs:674` calls it with a unit id, so a host-qualified id goes through the one address home rather than being colon-joined a second time; the `satisfies`-slot comment above it (2153-2156) states the corpus-wide `kind:name` keying this entry retires for a file child.

`render_node` calls the lifted home rather than re-deciding the same split; `member_lookup`'s bare-key fallback now also reaches a nested *file* child, which is the behavior the grammar asks for — a bare key resolves only when one host carries it.
The layout-member site's member address goes through the one home, so a layout-bearing file child is named by its whole address.
`features` matches its nested-member rows by this member's address; the match goes through the one home so a file child that itself composes an embedded body still finds its rows.

`explain` resolves a file child at `<host-address>/<kind>/<key>` (the target parse at the address split, and the by-kind fallbacks that spell a bare name), and `narrate_address_form`'s standing claim — 'a file child's declaration row carries the same host-qualified address an embedded member's does' — becomes true rather than aspirational.

No change expected: `member_address_coincidence` counts `Features::id` per kind, so host-qualified ids make two same-named children under different hosts two addresses rather than one coincidence. Listed because its inline tests exercise that function over composed ids.

Two hosts each carrying a same-named file child are two members at two addresses — no `member.admissibility` coincidence — and a child resolves at its host-qualified address, not at a bare `kind:name`.
`explain '<host-kind>:<host>/<child-kind>/<key>'` resolves a nested file child; the bare key resolves only while one host carries it.

tests.asserts: two hosts each carrying a `home` file child compose two distinct addresses and report no coincidence
`explain` resolves a file child at its host-qualified address, and refuses a bare key several hosts carry by naming them

acceptance: `cargo test` green, with the two hosts/one child-name corpus checking clean instead of reporting a `member.admissibility` coincidence, and `explain` resolving the host-qualified address.
